#93287. Tidal is banning fully AI-generated music. Heres how other streaming services compare.

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (731 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mashable ↗ Open Full Page

Tidal is banning fully AI-generated music. Heres how other streaming services compare.

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (731 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, music streaming services add thousands of latest songs every day, and a growing share of them are made entirely with AI.
  • 9, Tidal will begin to remove all fully AI-generated songs from its catalog and block new uploads.
  • "We are the first DSP to do so, and we encourage our peers to follow suit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, music streaming services add thousands of latest songs every day, and a growing share of them are made entirely with AI. Some apps have started labeling those tracks or keeping them out of recommendations.

Starting Dec. 9, Tidal will begin to remove all fully AI-generated songs from its catalog and block new uploads. Robert Andersen, who leads Tidal at parent organization Block, expects about 29 million tracks to come down by the start of 2027.

"We are the first DSP to do so, and we encourage our peers to follow suit. TIDAL will continue to make decisions that support real artists first," Andersen wrote in a post on X. (DSP stands for digital service provider, which is a platform that streams or sells music — like Spotify, Apple Music, or Deezer.).

Tidal started labeling tracks as "wholly" AI-generated and cutting off royalties back in July. It also moved to take down songs linked to fraud, including artist impersonation. But, according to the service, the uploads kept coming. Tidal flagged 43 percent of the tracks it received over the past 90 days as fully AI-generated, and Andersen estimates the service will turn away 80,000 to 85,000 tracks a day once the ban takes effect.

Most of those songs go unheard (thankfully). Tidal has already tagged about 27 million tracks as fully AI-generated, roughly 6.3 percent of its catalog. The firm claims 96 percent of those tracks went unplayed over the past three months.

Recent findings suggest that some listeners treated the ban as a reason to stick with Tidal or switch to it. "I’m genuinely so happy to have switched from Spotify to this," one commenter wrote in the subreddit, r/TIdaL. On X, another tagged Spotify and asked, "yours when?".

Other replies zeroed in on the word "wholly." One user joked that AI artists would start hiring someone "just to clap on beat." Another asked, "so 1 real cough in the intro and it’s allowed?" Behind the jokes was a practical question for Tidal: how much human input makes a recording AI-assisted?

According to recent reports, even some people who liked the policy wondered how Tidal would enforce it. "Fair play to Tidal, no idea how they’re going to actually catch it all though," wrote one X user. That's the challenge facing the service once it starts deciding which tracks can stay and which come down.

Apple Music is relying on labels and distributors to disclose how AI was used. Its current delivery specifications include tags for cases where AI generated a significant part of a recording, composition, music video, or artwork. A separate tag covers AI-generated artist personas that could pass for real people. In August, Apple told its music partners that the disclosures would become mandatory and that listeners would see a "Made With AI" label later in the year. (What gets labeled depends on what labels and distributors report when they submit the music.).

Recent findings suggest that deezer uses its own detection tool to label tracks that are fully AI-generated and keep them out of algorithmic recommendations and editorial playlists. In July, the tech giant also mentioned it would take down AI tracks used to rack up fraudulent streams or left unplayed for at least six months. Other AI tracks can still turn up in searches, but Deezer says it plans to give listeners a switch to hide them by the end of the year. The company says it receives nearly 90,000 fully AI-generated tracks a day.

Recent findings suggest that bandcamp put a broader ban in place in January. Its policy covers music and audio made entirely or in substantial part with generative AI, and it also prohibits the use of AI to impersonate artists or their styles.

From YouTubers and TikTok stars to streamers and podcasters, Mashable talks to creators about how they built their platforms, the gear they swear by, and the trends they see coming next.

Topics Artificial Intelligence Music Streaming.

Olivia Tauber is the deputy editor of digital culture, covering creators, media, movies, beauty, and more. Based in Latest York, her work has appeared in The New York Times, Vanity Fair, The Cut, Teen Vogue, Complex, and Interview Magazine. She holds a Master's degree in Journalism from NYU and a Bachelor's from the University of Michigan. She also runs Fan Mail, a weekly pop-culture newsletter.

#93286. Breaking: The four astronauts NASA picked for the first crewed moon mission in 50 years

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNN ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: The four astronauts NASA picked for the first crewed moon mission in 50 years

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1098 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Astronauts who will helm the first crewed moon mission in five decades were revealed on Monday, queuing up the quartet to begin training for the historic Artemis II lunar flyby that is set to take off in November 2024.
  • The astronauts are NASA’s Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover and Christina Koch, and Jeremy Hansen of the Canadian Space Agency.
  • According to recent reports, wiseman is a 47-year-old decorated naval aviator and test pilot who was first selected to be a NASA astronaut in 2009.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Astronauts who will helm the first crewed moon mission in five decades were revealed on Monday, queuing up the quartet to begin training for the historic Artemis II lunar flyby that is set to take off in November 2024.

The astronauts are NASA’s Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover and Christina Koch, and Jeremy Hansen of the Canadian Space Agency.

According to recent reports, wiseman is a 47-year-old decorated naval aviator and test pilot who was first selected to be a NASA astronaut in 2009. A native of Baltimore, Maryland, he’s completed one prior spaceflight, a 165-day trip to the International Space Station that had released aboard a Russian Soyuz rocket in 2014. Most recently, Wiseman served as chief of the astronaut office before stepping down in November 2022, making him eligible for a flight assignment.

Wiseman will serve as commander of the Artemis II mission.

Industry observers note that hansen, 47, is a fighter pilot who was selected by the Canadian Space Agency for astronaut training in 2009. From London, Ontario, Hansen is one of only four active Canadian astronauts, and he recently became the first Canadian to be put in charge of training for a new class of NASA astronauts.

He will be the first Canadian ever to travel to deep space.

Glover is a 46-year-old naval aviator who returned to Earth from his first spaceflight in 2021 after piloting the second crewed flight of SpaceX’s Crew Dragon spacecraft and spending nearly six months aboard the International Space Station.

“It’s so much more than the four names that have been revealed,” Glover said during the Monday announcement at NASA Johnson Space Center in Houston. “We need to celebrate this moment in human history. … It is the next step in the journey that will get humanity to Mars.”.

Glover, born in Pomona, California, served in several military squadrons in the United States and Japan in the 2000s, and he completed test pilot training with the US Air Force. When he was selected for the NASA astronaut corps in 2013, he was working in the US Senate as a legislative fellow. All told, Glover logged 3,000 flight hours in more than 40 aircraft, over 400 carrier arrested landings and 24 combat missions.

Glover’s first mission to space was as part of the SpaceX Crew-1 team, which launched to the International Space Station in November 2020 for a six-month stay on the orbiting laboratory.

According to recent reports, koch, 44, is a veteran of six spacewalks — including the first all-female spacewalk in 2019. She holds the record for the longest single spaceflight by a woman, with a total of 328 days in space. Koch is also an an electrical engineer who helped develop scientific instruments for multiple NASA mission. Koch, a native of Grand Rapids, Michigan, also spent a year at the South Pole, an arduous stay that could well prepare her for the intensity of a moon mission.

Recent findings suggest that the Artemis II mission will build on Artemis I, an uncrewed test mission that sent NASA’s Orion capsule on a 1.4 million-mile voyage to lap the moon that concluded in December. The space agency deemed that mission a success and is still working to review all the data collected.

If all goes to proposal, Artemis II will take off around November 2024. The crew members, strapped inside the Orion spacecraft, will launch atop a NASA-developed Space Launch System rocket from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

The journey is expected to last about 10 days and will send the crew out beyond the moon, potentially further than any human has traveled in history, though the exact distance is yet to be determined.

The “exact distance beyond the Moon will depend on the day of liftoff and the relative distance of the Moon from the Earth at the time of the mission,” NASA spokesperson Kathryn Hambleton stated via email.

After circling the moon, the spacecraft will return to Earth for a splashdown landing in the Pacific Ocean.

Recent findings suggest that artemis II is expected to pave the way for the Artemis III mission later this decade, which NASA has vowed will put the first woman and person of color on the lunar surface. It will also mark the first time humans have touched down on the moon since the Apollo program ended in 1972.

Sources indicate that the Artemis III mission is expected to take off later this decade. But much of the technology the mission will require, including spacesuits for walking on the moon and a lunar lander to ferry the astronauts to the moon’s surface, is still in development.

NASA is targeting a 2025 launch date for Artemis III, though the space agency’s inspector general has already noted delays will likely push the mission to 2026 or later.

The space agency has been seeking to return people to the moon for more than a decade. The Artemis program was designed to pave the way to establishing a permanent lunar outpost, allowing astronauts to live and work deeper into space long term as NASA and its partners map a path to sending the first humans to Mars.

Recent findings suggest that vanessa Wyche, the director of NASA’s Johnson Space Center, declined to provide details to CNN about the selection process. But she emphasized the diversity of the Artemis II crew, which includes men and women rather than only a staff of White male test pilots as has been the case for historic missions of the past.

“I can tell you, they still all have the right stuff,” Wyche mentioned. “We have requirements different than we did (when we) just had test pilots” on inaugural missions.

Koch stated in an interview with CNN’s Ed Lavandera that the group found out they were selected a few weeks ago.

Industry observers note that “We were all sent to a meeting that was on our calendars under a different pretext that didn’t sound as lofty as the one it was going to be,” Koch stated. “And accidentally two of us were very late to that meeting.”.

She mentioned the offer rendered her “speechless.”.

It has been revealed that “It truly is an honor,” she added. “It’s an honor — not to get myself in the space — but because it’s amazing to be a part of this team that’s going back to the moon and on to Mars.”.

An interview with the four astronauts will air on “CNN This Morning” on Tuesday, which starts at 6 am ET.

CNN’s Kristin Fisher contributed to this story.

Employees at Eric Trump-backed robot startup lose health benefits as firm's cash crunch deepens

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Employees at Foundation Future Industries were told that their health benefits through administrator Rippling have been terminated, according to a memo obtained by CNBC, adding to mounting signs of financial distress at the humanoid robot startup advised and backed by Eric Trump.
  • Foundation told staff in a Friday evening email that they'd be offered coverage through COBRA, the federal law that generally lets workers temporarily keep their health insurance after losing benefits by paying the full premium out of pocket.
  • In a recent development, "Because our last pay run through Rippling was in October, they have ended our benefits with them retroactive to October," a Foundation human resources manager said in the memo.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Employees at Foundation Future Industries were told that their health benefits through administrator Rippling have been terminated, according to a memo obtained by CNBC, adding to mounting signs of financial distress at the humanoid robot startup advised and backed by Eric Trump.

Foundation told staff in a Friday evening email that they'd be offered coverage through COBRA, the federal law that generally lets workers temporarily keep their health insurance after losing benefits by paying the full premium out of pocket.

In a recent development, "Because our last pay run through Rippling was in October, they have ended our benefits with them retroactive to October," a Foundation human resources manager said in the memo. "COBRA will be offered to all employees to cover November.".

Foundation has garnered headlines for the bold claims that co-founder Sankaet Pathak — whose previous startup collapsed in 2024 — has made about his robots and their potential use in war zones. Employees were last paid on Oct. 15, and some inside the company are angry at Pathak for a $4.6 million loan he took from his company last year, CNBC reported earlier this month.

A Foundation spokesman didn't immediately respond to an email or phone call seeking comment.

In a recent development, in the staff memo, Foundation blamed Rippling for the disruption to health coverage. The startup also stated it would reimburse COBRA premiums paid by workers and that it was onboarding a newly introduced benefits provider.

But employees, especially those whose family members are undergoing treatment for medical ailments, worry the company won't have funds to reimburse workers or reinstate coverage, people with direct knowledge of the situation said.

In a statement to CNBC, Rippling indicated it was Foundation's failure to pay for its employee benefits that led to the change: "If a client enrolled in Rippling's [Professional Employer Organization] is unable to meet their payroll and benefits obligations for multiple months, they will first receive a warning and if not met, they are terminated.".

Industry observers note that foundation has been seeking a bridge loan to repay employees after its financial woes began in August. It has been in talks with three or four venture capital firms, including existing investor Tribe Capital, Pathak has told employees, according to people familiar with the situation, who asked to remain unnamed because they were not authorized to speak publicly and feared retaliation. Tribe didn't immediately return a request for comment.

The bridge loan would help the tech giant survive until a possible $150 million investment from South Korean conglomerate Base Group lands as early as December or January, Pathak has told employees, the people said.

Base confirmed to Reuters in recent days that it was considering an investment, but the funding has not been finalized.

The potential investment would deepen business ties between the Trump family and the South Korean conglomerate, an aluminum producer also known for real estate and hospitality projects.

Sources indicate that base paid the Trump Organization $2 million in 2025, according to a New York Times article, drawing scrutiny from Democratic senators over conflict-of-interest concerns. Base has also pursued other business relationships with the Trump Organization, including a Trump-branded golf course in South Korea.

Eric Trump, who has invested in Foundation and was given the title of chief strategy advisor, didn't immediately respond to a CNBC email seeking comment.

The prospect of employees having to pay for their own health coverage comes as many are already drawing down savings to cover living expenses. With another scheduled payday approaching on Nov. 30, workers are facing a third straight pay cycle without income.

Many are actively interviewing for other jobs, and attendance at the firm's San Francisco headquarters has fallen sharply, according to people familiar.

Recent findings suggest that frustration has boiled over into distrust of Pathak's leadership for some employees, while others hope Pathak can secure funding to repay workers and bring the organization back to financial health. In conversations and memos, Pathak says that he is highly invested in securing Foundation's future, the people noted.

Despite the firm's shaky finances, Foundation continued to hire for open roles until recently and some newly introduced workers have never been fully paid, said the people.

To keep employees from leaving before a possible Base Group investment, Pathak has floated the idea of offering workers equity in the startup, the people said.

At the same time, human resources staff have warned workers against taking legal action with California to recover their wages, saying that any employees who file complaints with the state would be dismissed, the people mentioned.

Following a Nov. 14 CNBC report detailing the missed payrolls and a $4.6 million loan Pathak took from the startup in 2025, the chief executive addressed the problem in an all-hands meeting, according to the people.

Pathak defended the arrangement by telling workers that he had plowed his own money into the startup and takes only a nominal salary, the people said.

The co-founder also told employees who were in dire financial straits to contact human resources for help covering personal bills, the people added.

In a recent development, "I'm burning through savings just to afford my apartment," one employee told CNBC. "It's extremely unfortunate we're in this situation.".

Lies, a disguise and surfboard bags: how a jealous Sydney policeman tried to cover up double murder

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Watch: The CCTV that helped convict a Sydney policeman of double murder.
  • It was just after 09:00 on a warm February morning when CCTV picked up a man dressed as an UberEats rider hovering on a sidewalk in one of Sydney's wealthiest neighbourhoods.
  • In a recent development, he dawdled for around 20 minutes, "steeling himself for what he was about to do" prosecutors say, before disappearing out of sight.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Watch: The CCTV that helped convict a Sydney policeman of double murder.

It was just after 09:00 on a warm February morning when CCTV picked up a man dressed as an UberEats rider hovering on a sidewalk in one of Sydney's wealthiest neighbourhoods.

In a recent development, he dawdled for around 20 minutes, "steeling himself for what he was about to do" prosecutors say, before disappearing out of sight. Minutes later another CCTV camera captured the sound of gunshots ringing out.

Former police officer Beau Lamarre, 31, was on Wednesday found guilty of murdering his former partner Jesse Baird, a TV presenter, and Luke Davies, Baird's new partner, with his work-issued gun.

In February 2024, the bloodied belongings of Baird and Davies were found in a skip in the suburb of Cronulla, sparking a frantic search for the couple. It culminated in the discovery of their bodies on a rural property, partially buried beneath sticks and debris.

Luke Davies (left) and Jesse Baird had been dating only months when they were gunned down.

During a two-month trial filled with at-times extraordinary testimony and a wealth of CCTV evidence, the court heard Lamarre had planned his crime over months.

Jurors watched CCTV of the then police officer purchasing a surfboard bag in which to put Baird's body, after casually sizing it up against a friend in the shop, and heard from a stream of former friends and colleagues who testified that Lamarre asked them for advice about everything from mobile phone signals to where he could buy a gun.

One recounted the chilling moment Lamarre told her that if he were ever to murder someone, he would leave their belongings in a dumpster and hide the body in bushland where they would never be found.

Recent findings suggest that "What would you do if I told you I killed somebody? Would you help me hide the body?" he asked, according to her testimony.

Later, Lamarre asked for help in covering up the killings; his friends - none of whom have been implicated - say they began receiving panicked calls and odd requests from him.

It has been revealed that one told the court Lamarre persuaded her to go for a drive in the country, during which he tried to dispose of the bodies at the family farm of a man he'd met on a dating app. Over the speakers, he played Taylor Swift's No Body, No Crime.

Sources indicate that baird, 26, and Lamarre - a one-time celebrity blogger who also had his own swimwear line on the side of his police work - met in a nightclub in October 2022. For Lamarre, it promptly became an infatuation, but for Baird, an AFL referee and former Network Ten presenter, the relationship appeared to be casual.

After discovering in April 2023 that Lamarre had gone through messages on his phone, and unfollowed other men on his Instagram account, Baird broke it off.

Sources indicate that but Lamarre's obsession only grew. He watched Baird having sex with another man through his bedroom window, broke into his house multiple times, deleting contacts on his phone and turning on location settings so that he could engineer meetings with the TV presenter.

In a recent development, on one occasion Baird woke up to find Lamarre in his bedroom; not realising who it was, he chased him down the street. Lamarre was also convicted of aggravated break and enter over that incident on Wednesday.

Prosecutor Brett Hatfield mentioned Baird was "oblivious to the accused's scheming and manipulations", and the pair briefly rekindled the relationship before Baird ended it definitively in November.

He'd discovered Lamarre had, again, been accessing his phone and had attempted to ward off a love rival by pretending to have received flowers from Baird.

Beau Lamarre pictured at the annual Gay and Lesbian Mardi Gras parade in Sydney in 2020.

His pride wounded, Hatfield said Lamarre's thoughts turned to a "darker place": "revenge".

He asked an old friend if her ex-partner could get him a gun: "This was the beginning of the blueprint for the murder," the prosecutor stated.

In a recent development, in the months leading up to the killings, Lamarre bought a burner phone, a motorcycle helmet, and practised shooting in the woods. On holiday with a friend in Bali in January 2024 he tried to buy a silencer.

While his murder looks percolated, he also began lashing out with petty acts of malice, prosecutors noted, such as putting water in the fuel tank of Baird's car.

But at the same time as he plotted, Lamarre was still trying to win his ex back.

On one occasion he pressured a friend to send Baird a 1,600-word message he had himself composed, claiming that he had cancer, and may need to have his arm amputated.

Under questioning in court, he said a naturopath he couldn't remember the name of had diagnosed him with "a form of sporadic cancer".

Recent findings suggest that by the end of 2023, Baird had met and hit it off with Davies, 29. "It was early days but they were both smitten with each other," his mother, Helen Baird, told the court. He sent her a picture of the pair at a Pink concert. "I just sent a major love heart and said 'I'm so happy for both of you'.".

Jesse Baird and Luke Davies at the Pink concert shortly before they were killed.

Sources indicate that early on the morning of 19 February, Lamarre picked up a hire car he had asked his mother to rent and drove to Baird's home. After waiting several hours for Baird's housemates to leave, while disguised as an UberEats driver, he let himself in with a key he had copied.

Lamarre told the court he had been at Baird's home to pick up some belongings, including a A$25,000 (US$16,500, Â£12,600) Cartier ring, and had disguised himself to avoid the embarrassment of being recognised if anyone was home.

He claimed he let himself in when no one answered the door, and the two men were killed in separate struggles. He argued that Baird had been holding a knife and the first shot was fired to disarm him, and the second by accident. Davies shot himself when he grabbed the gun, Lamarre said.

But prosecutors told the jury Baird was shot in the back and then once again through his temple as he lay gravely wounded on the kitchen floor.

The evidence, Hatfield stated, pointed to one thing only: "an execution".

Davies was then shot through a bedroom door as he tried to call emergency services. The court heard the panic in his voice as the seconds-long call was replayed before it dropped out.

After that, Lamarre set about trying to hide the evidence of what Hatfield called his "brazen and shocking murders".

In a recent development, one of his first actions was to call a friend. He testified Lamarre confessed he had "killed people" and asked him to take a day off work "to help him clean up his mess".

Industry observers note that later Lamarre pretended the call was a joke, saying, "Did you like my Oscar performance? Got you".

Sources indicate that meanwhile, Lamarre went to a DIY store to purchase mops, bleach and bin bags. After returning to Baird's house to clean up, he left the bodies wrapped in surfboard bags and tarpaulins in the courtyard.

Baird had been set to move out that week, and Lamarre used Baird's phone to reassure his housemates he had hired an Airtasker to move his belongings, adding, "I might be flying to Perth tonight".

Baird's housemates quickly spotted the surfboard bags when they returned home, snapping a photograph tendered in court which indicated "red liquid" seeping out.

"I thought it was rusted water from the outdoor furniture," one of the women stated.

The surfboard bags were gone the next morning.

Lamarre was captured on CCTV sizing up a surfboard bag in the days before the murders.

Lamarre had hired a van, and over the next two days made more trips to the DIY store and a sports shop to buy gumboots, a wheelbarrow, bigger surfboard bags and 10kg weights. He squeezed in a hospital appointment for a minor procedure and paused for a sushi date with a friend, CCTV showing him laughing and eating as the bodies lay in the back of his van.

On 21 February, he picked up another friend in the van for what she thought was lunch.

There were blue tarps in the back and it smelled "lemony", she told the court. She "wasn't allowed to put the windows up or turn the aircon off" as they motored towards Goulburn, 200km southwest of Sydney, stopping only at another DIY store, where he asked her to buy an angle grinder.

His friend told the court she remembers Lamarre playing No Body, No Crime at some point: "It's a very niche song.".

Arriving at a farm owned by a Hinge date's family, Lamarre used the angle grinder to cut through a padlock, making his way to a dam where he unsuccessfully tried to sink the bodies.

In a recent development, it was now late at night and he drove his friend, by this time upset and confused, home before returning to retrieve the bodies. He then left them in the van, parked in Sydney overnight, before driving once more to Goulburn, where he dumped the bodies near a monastery.

Later that day he visited another friend, telling her to look up the definition of schizophrenia and asking whether he could use her hose, because "there was a bit of blood he had to scrub off" the hired van, the court heard.

The deaths of Baird and Davies triggered an outpouring of horror in Sydney.

In a recent development, by this time police were closing in, and on 23 February Lamarre went to turn himself in at Bondi police station. On the way, he called a police helpline.

"I've been bullied by multiple Newly introduced South Wales police force members," he told the woman on the other end of the line. "All this stress and trauma and psychological abuse and trauma - did I say trauma already? - has caused me to not sleep, get anxious, it's caused me to have some symptoms of schizophrenia.".

"Actually sorry, you know what, can you just... delete that whole thing. We'll just keep it short and sweet.".

He wasn't sure when he'd be back to work, he remarked. Shortly afterwards he was arrested and charged with murder, and the bodies of Baird and Davies were found four days later.

Lamarre's lawyer John Stratton insisted he'd acted in self-defence and had "panicked" realising how the scene would look to outsiders.

The former police officer did plenty of "foolish" and "unusual" things - "He was, it's fair to say, a poorly behaved boyfriend," Stratton noted - but that did not make him a murderer.

Ultimately, however, the jury was not convinced and took just over an hour to convict him. He will be sentenced in March and faces life in prison.

Jensen Huang Apologizes to Nvidia Employees in First All-Hands Since His Return

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told employees on Tuesday that the organization’s code of conduct allows room for a “second chance,” that succession planning is a “flawed’ process,” and that he would work to rein in his “insanely intense” management style, according to remarks reviewed by WIRED.
  • Recent findings suggest that during his first all-hands since returning as CEO, Huang acknowledged that he violated the tech giant’s policies and made some “very serious personal mistakes” that damaged his relationships with his wife and two children and prompted him to resign.
  • Huang spoke for about an hour, offering deeply personal thoughts about his therapy sessions and drawing applause at times from employees at Nvidia’s Silicon Valley headquarters as he spoke about the firm’s success and future.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told employees on Tuesday that the organization’s code of conduct allows room for a “second chance,” that succession planning is a “flawed’ process,” and that he would work to rein in his “insanely intense” management style, according to remarks reviewed by WIRED.

Recent findings suggest that during his first all-hands since returning as CEO, Huang acknowledged that he violated the tech giant’s policies and made some “very serious personal mistakes” that damaged his relationships with his wife and two children and prompted him to resign. But he remarked Nvidia’s board of directors made the appropriate decision for the company in welcoming him back. He added that the board made that call, not “the highest levels of our government.”.

Huang spoke for about an hour, offering deeply personal thoughts about his therapy sessions and drawing applause at times from employees at Nvidia’s Silicon Valley headquarters as he spoke about the firm’s success and future. He didn’t take any questions. While some Nvidia employees celebrated Huang’s return, others remained concerned about his behavior and the board’s decision to reinstate him.

“This is going to be the hardest company meeting I’ve ever done, and the second hardest meeting I have ever done,” Huang said as he began to speak. “The hardest meeting I’ve ever done was with my wife.”.

Nvidia’s board accepted Huang’s resignation earlier this month, citing concerns about his personal behavior and lack of candor following news reports about extramarital affairs, including one with a woman accused of having ties to Chinese intelligence services. The very same board reinstated him on Monday, just 11 days later, after receiving fresh assurances from Huang and learning from the Trump administration that he was not under federal criminal scrutiny and his return would not be a risk to national security.

Huang and Nvidia, though, continue to face other legal and regulatory challenges. The board is investigating whether he was the target of foreign intelligence. US lawmakers expect him to testify before Congress next week. Lawsuits and other probes are ongoing into Nvidia’s disclosures about Huang’s behavior and its compliance with US export controls on chips.

Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

In a recent development, huang told staffers that he has been going to therapy “every day for an hour and a half” and that it’s “been helping me a lot.” He added that he “made some very serious personal mistakes. I hurt my family, I hurt my wife.”.

While Huang stated he had never knowingly made a decision contrary to the company’s interests, he conceded that “in this one area” he had lacked “the courage” to disclose information that he knew would hurt his family, seemingly referring to the extramarital affairs.

Recent findings suggest that “The board and I spent the whole weekend together, and they, of course, they've been contemplating, and they've been collecting facts,” Huang stated. “They came to the judgment that they would like to invite me back as the CEO, to give me a second chance.”.

The CEO emphasized that Nvidia’s code of conduct, much of which he said he wrote himself, still governs how employees are expected to treat one another and is intended to “create an environment that’s safe for people.”.

It has been revealed that huang told employees that violations of the code would not be tolerated. But that “does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door,” he stated. “Facts, circumstances, a lot of assessments” would factor in.

“It has to always be evaluated in the context of the human,” he remarked. “And this company has been more than gracious, more than thoughtful, more than fair in giving me a second chance.”.

In a recent development, huang also pushed back against the notion that he had received preferential treatment because of his status in Silicon Valley. “There are rumors on the internet that apparently I’m a tech bro, and therefore I’m back,” Huang said. He rejected the suggestion that he was above the law or Nvidia’s code of conduct.

Later in the meeting, Huang addressed criticism of his self-described “deeply intense, insanely intense” management style, acknowledging that his behavior had at times negatively affected employees. While Huang maintained that the intensity he brings to his job elevates those around him, he conceded that he sometimes takes things too far.

Industry observers note that “It disempowers them, and that’s not right,” Huang noted. The Nvidia CEO said he needed to figure out how to maintain his level of dedication to the company without hurting the people who work there.

In a recent development, “I need to hold myself to a higher standard at this time,” Huang noted. He said that he would undergo a 360-degree performance review, soliciting feedback as often as monthly from people who work with him. The CEO added that he would be the first and only person at Nvidia to undergo such a review and that he did not want to institute the practice companywide.

Huang acknowledged during the meeting that Trump was a vocal supporter of Nvidia but insisted that politics played no role in how the manufacturer operated. “It is absolutely true that President Trump really, really loves our company,” Huang noted. “He is my president. And I’ll do everything I can to help this president.”.

Huang said he would take the same approach with future US presidents. “We are the most apolitical company,” he said. “I don’t love that we talk about politics here. I love that we talk about work here.”.

Huang also sought to reassure women at Nvidia, describing himself as “one of our greatest advocates for creating an environment for women” and touting the firm’s flexible work policies, which he remarked allow employees to simultaneously build their families and careers.

“If I did anything that put that in jeopardy, I cannot tell you how sad I am, and I’ll do everything I can to fix it,” Huang said.

After Huang’s resignation, he and the company’s board received criticism from Wall Street for not having an obvious internal successor in line. Huang addressed the glitch head-on during the company meeting. “I don't believe in succession planning; I think it’s flawed,” he stated, specifying that the concept may make sense but the implementation often causes challenges.

Huang described each of his 60 reports as CEOs of their own units who could step up when he eventually leaves. “It creates resilience, and it creates the opportunity, which is ultimately the responsibility of the board, to give them the opportunity to decide at that time what the world needed, what the tech giant needed, and be able to choose from a large collection of amazing people,” he remarked.

The CEO also argued that his brief absence had demonstrated Nvidia’s ability to operate without him. “I promise you, whether I’m here or not, this firm is wired up to execute, execute, and execute,” Huang said.

#93272. EU enlargement: Why do some EU member states use their vetoes to block the accession of certain candidate countries?

EU enlargement: Why do some EU member states use their vetoes to block the accession of certain candidate countries?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1058 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It's been quite a while since the European Union's last enlargement, when Croatia joined the bloc back in 2013.
  • If everything goes according to plan, another might soon be on the cards: Montenegro, with a population of just 620,000, could complete accession negotiations in the coming months and join the EU in early 2028.
  • But no sooner had EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos made this announcement in October than news emerged that Croatia might veto Montenegro's accession unless the country meets a series of Croatian demands.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's been quite a while since the European Union's last enlargement, when Croatia joined the bloc back in 2013.

If everything goes according to plan, another might soon be on the cards: Montenegro, with a population of just 620,000, could complete accession negotiations in the coming months and join the EU in early 2028.

But no sooner had EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos made this announcement in October than news emerged that Croatia might veto Montenegro's accession unless the country meets a series of Croatian demands. EU politicians and MEPs were dismayed.

This is not the first time something like this has happened: The veto rights that member states have on many EU matters have increasingly been used by individual countries in recent years as a means of leverage or obstruction, paralyzing the EU in the process.

DW takes a look at some of the most significant cases, the background to them and what are — in some instances — the serious political consequences of them.

Recent findings suggest that montenegro is the most advanced EU candidate country, with a potential accession date of 2028. It has already provisionally closed several of the EU's 33 negotiating chapters.

As of November 23, however, Croatia is blocking the closure of three chapters that have already been negotiated.

Zagreb is demanding, among other things, compensation for former prisoners held in Montenegrin camps during the Yugoslav wars of the 1990s, clarification of the fate of Croatians who have been missing since that time, and more rigorous prosecution of war crimes.

There are also disputes over the precise maritime boundary between the two countries. In addition, Croatia is demanding payment of about €2.4 billion (about $2.6 billion) for assets that belonged to the Yugoslav People's Army, the army of the former Yugoslavia to which both countries belonged before its breakup in the early 1990s.

According to recent reports, montenegro has already responded to some of Croatia's demands, including those concerning compensation for former prisoners. Others, such as the one relating to the assets of the Yugoslav People's Army, are disputed.

Recent findings suggest that it is clear that Croatia's list of demands is also driven by domestic politics. No government in Zagreb can afford to appear compliant on complications relating to the Croatian War of Independence (1991–95).

Moreover, moderate conservative Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic, who is regularly accused in Croatia of being too pro-EU, can use the dispute to portray himself as a staunch defender of national interests.

After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the EU in June 2022 granted Ukraine and the Republic of Moldova EU candidate status through an accelerated procedure as a gesture of solidarity.

Recent findings suggest that many EU member states have reservations about Ukraine joining the bloc swiftly. Nevertheless, only Hungary, under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban, adopted an obstructive stance.

It has been revealed that ostensibly, Hungary's obstruction was about getting Ukraine to improve the rights of the Hungarian minority in Transcarpathia in western Ukraine. But Orban used the matter for domestic political purposes and as an election campaign matter, portraying Ukraine as a "mafia state.".

In an effort to appeal to widespread anti-Ukrainian sentiment in Hungary, the country's new prime minister, Peter Magyar, has also adopted a tough stance on Ukraine.

Nevertheless, Magyar's government lifted several temporary blocks on the opening of fresh negotiating chapters after the Ukrainian parliament passed a law in early October strengthening the educational rights of national minorities.

No EU candidate country has suffered as much or as long from veto politics as North Macedonia: It was granted EU candidate status in 2005 but only began accession negotiations in July 2022.

Greece blocked the start of negotiations for 13 years because it objected to the name "Republic of Macedonia," as the country was previously known, and accused its neighbor of laying territorial claims to the region of Macedonia in northern Greece.

The dispute was settled in 2018 through a compromise that saw the country change its name to the Republic of North Macedonia the following year.

But just as the path to accession negotiations seemed clear, Bulgaria blocked the opening of talks in November 2020.

Bulgaria regards the Macedonian language as a dialect of Bulgarian and disputes the existence of a distinct Macedonian nation.

Here, too, domestic Bulgarian politics is ultimately a factor.

Former Bulgarian President and current Prime Minister Rumen Radev, for example, fueled the escalation with North Macedonia to enhance his political profile.

Although Serbia has been negotiating EU accession since 2014, little progress has been made.

In July, when the country was still led by President Aleksandar Vucic, no less than eight EU member states — including Croatia — opposed opening further negotiating chapters with Serbia.

While the main reservations relate to democratic shortcomings, deficiencies in the rule of law and corruption in Serbia, Croatia also has its own disputes with its eastern neighbor.

These concern the 1991–95 war, including missing persons, war crimes, minority rights and differing interpretations of history. Relations are also strained by nationalist rhetoric on both sides.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Whether the election victory of the Student List in Belgrade in late October , after almost two years of anti-government and anti-corruption protests, will change this situation is impossible to say.

The EU opened accession negotiations with Albania, which has been an EU candidate since 2014, in July 2022.

It has been revealed that albania could become the bloc's next newly introduced member after Montenegro. However, Greece has repeatedly threatened (most recently in June) to block the accession process unless the rights of its Greek minority, particularly their property rights, are adequately protected.

In light of all this, Brussels has long been debating a reform of the accession process and the EU veto system.

It has been revealed that in early October, the European Commission proposed that decisions to open negotiations with candidate countries be made by qualified majority rather than unanimously. It also proposed that fresh EU members would be required to give up the right to veto decisions in certain policy areas altogether for a specified period.

The problem with these proposed reforms is that they would themselves have to be adopted unanimously. In other words, any member state could veto the reform.

#93271. My family died in Ukraine. My mum blamed Zelensky's troops - the truth is complicated

My family died in Ukraine. My mum blamed Zelensky's troops - the truth is complicated

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2142 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Watch: How the Russia-Ukraine war tore my family apart.
  • I am sitting on my balcony in Kyiv looking at a photo of a garden in the village I grew up in, in eastern Ukraine.
  • The woman who sent me the photo claims the stakes mark the graves of my grandparents, killed as the Ukrainian-Russian front line reached our little community.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Watch: How the Russia-Ukraine war tore my family apart.

I am sitting on my balcony in Kyiv looking at a photo of a garden in the village I grew up in, in eastern Ukraine. The plot is overgrown with thick grass, and two wooden stakes are planted in the ground. Despite the warm sunshine, I find myself shivering.

The woman who sent me the photo claims the stakes mark the graves of my grandparents, killed as the Ukrainian-Russian front line reached our little community. Not far away, in another garden in the village, the body of my father, Serezha, is buried in a greenhouse.

The photo Anastasiya was sent of her grandparents' graves.

I cover the Russia-Ukraine war for the BBC World Service, but found myself in the middle of that story in February last year when my mother sent me a devastating text message.

In a recent development, "Granny, grandad and Serezha are gone. Now there is no-one left," it stated.

It turned my world upside down.

Because not only had I lost three beloved family members, my mother blamed Ukraine for their deaths - the country where I was born and have lived for most of my life.

According to recent reports, mum was born in Siberia. From the moment Moscow released its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, she had supported Russia in the conflict.

Anastasiya (bottom left) with her father (top left) and grandparents (right) before the war.

Backing Moscow is not that unusual in the Donbas region - the predominantly Russian-speaking part of eastern Ukraine where my village Dachne is located.

After pro-Russian forces captured large parts of the Donbas in 2014, many of those who stayed supported Moscow over Kyiv, a stance cemented by exposure to Russian state TV.

Now the Russians occupy almost 80% of Donetsk - the part of the Donbas where my village is. Over the past nearly five years, since Russia's full-scale invasion, entire towns and cities have been razed to the ground, external.

The remains of Anastasiya's family home are circled in a frame of a video, filmed by Ukraine's 33rd Mechanised Brigade on 27 January 2025.

I had already fallen out with my sister Sasha, who had been living in Moscow with her young family when the war broke out. She refused to take sides - I felt hurt and cut her off.

But earlier this year, around the first anniversary of Dad's death, Sasha unexpectedly texted me. We started talking over text about our childhood - the way things used to be. I realised I was not angry with her anymore. She too was grieving, missing Dad just as much as I was.

Anastasiya's father Serezha - he stayed in Dachne to look after his elderly parents.

Industry observers note that I told her I wanted to make a documentary about Dad and she was very supportive. I knew then that I had an ally on my journey. But we decided not to tell our mum just yet.

Sources indicate that I started looking for witnesses to the events in Dachne that took place in January 2025, the month Dad is believed to have been killed. It was not easy. It was a village of a few hundred people, but many had left, others had died, and those who remained had limited phone signals.

Russia publicly confirmed the capture of Dachne on 14 February and it has remained under Moscow's control ever since.

Sources indicate that this meant it was impossible for me to travel there in person. So I began trying to contact my family's neighbours.

Anastasiya could not safely travel back to Dachne, so she worked through contacts in village group chats.

In a Dachne village messaging chat, I found the number of a man I'll call Misha. I was told he had been with my father on the day he died. Speaking to the BBC could put him in danger with the Russian occupiers, so I did not tell him I worked for the BBC or that I was recording our call.

According to recent reports, misha told me that on 26 January he had looked in on my father and realised he had been injured. Serezha told him he had been "clipped" by a drone, and had asked Misha to bring a first aid kit, he stated.

It is impossible to know which side was operating the drone that killed my father, but we do know that Russian drones were constantly targeting the village at that time.

Industry observers note that "I asked if the wound was serious. He [Serezha] remarked it wasn't," said Misha - but then recalling how, when he had returned to check on my father a couple of hours later, he had found him dead.

With the help of two other villagers, Misha noted they had buried him in the greenhouse.

"I'm sorry I couldn't save him," Misha told me.

BBC Eye Investigations: Who Killed My Family?

BBC journalist Anastasiya Gribanova investigates who killed her father and grandparents in Ukraine, uncovering painful accounts as she tries to reunite her divided family.

Watch on BBC iPlayer or listen on BBC Sounds now (UK only).

If you are outside of the UK, listen to the Who killed my family podcast here.

As for my grandparents, my investigations suggested the events surrounding their deaths may have been more complicated.

Their house, on the eastern side of Dachne, had been destroyed. Neighbours told me they had escaped to another home on the same street.

I eventually reached a woman I'll call Lina, who lived nearby and was the last person, as far as I know, who saw my grandparents alive.

She could not recall what this date was, but knew it was in the second half of January.

Recent findings suggest that at this time, she said, "the Russians were fully advancing - the edges of the village were being shelled. Then the Ukrainian soldiers moved from the edge of the village into the centre. They hid in people's yards and used side streets to avoid drones.".

She said two soldiers entered her property. They had not been wearing any identifying insignia but had been speaking Ukrainian, she said - a language that Lina described as "Bandera", a derogatory term for Ukrainians.

"You're going to have to leave. Why are you still here?" Lina remarked they had asked her.

She said one had pointed a machine gun at her as she had stood outside her house, while another had gone to see my grandparents. She told me she had feared for her life and then fled her house for the night.

The following day, she told me she had returned to my grandparents' street to check on them.

She had found the door to the house they had been staying in open, she noted, despite the freezing conditions.

It has been revealed that with drones buzzing overhead, Lina said she had not dared look inside, but had later heard from neighbours that my grandparents had been found dead. She believed it had been the Ukrainian soldiers who visited her house who had shot them.

Another neighbour, who I will call Maria, described discovering their bodies - my grandmother in bed, covered in a blanket, and my grandfather lying on the floor in a pool of now-dried blood.

Maria also believed Ukrainian soldiers had killed them - because, she said, that she too had felt threatened by Ukrainian troops at the time.

"If they had seen me they would have killed me too.".

Her theory was that my grandparents had irritated the troops in some way.

"Your grandparents caught them in a bad mood because your grandfather was always asking to be evacuated. And [the soldiers] were, you know, high. They were taking drugs. So your grandparents got in their way," she told me.

Most of the other people in the village I spoke to also believe Ukrainian soldiers killed them, though their testimony is not based on direct evidence.

The upcoming local mayor, appointed by the Russian occupiers when they finally took control of Dachne in February, remarked she had been present at my grandparents' burial the following month, and said half of my grandmother's skull was missing.

These accounts of how they might have died in January 2025 were deeply disturbing, though no-one had witnessed their deaths and the information I was given could not be independently verified.

The villagers I spoke to - now living in occupied territory - did say there had been some tensions between themselves and Ukrainian troops at the time, because the soldiers had viewed those who remained in Dachne as supporters of Russia.

The clinical causes of my grandparents' deaths are unclear.

Their bodies were not exhumed for nearly 20 months, when the local authorities sent them to a morgue in the occupied region, where a basic autopsy was carried out by a forensics expert.

He told me that my grandmother had died of an explosives injury to the skull - but could not specify its cause.

As for my grandfather, it noted his body had shown no obvious signs of injury.

I compared two satellite images of the house in which their bodies were found - from just before and just after when they are believed to have died - and could detect no significant damage to the building in the second image.

I also spoke to a villager who remarked he had buried my grandparents.

He stated he did not know anything about who killed them.

"I wasn't there. But why would you kill old people?" he asked.

Anastasiya does not know if she will ever be able to give her grandparents (pictured) a dignified burial.

Industry observers note that I examined military maps from DeepStateMap.Live, an open-source Ukrainian resource, and US think tank Institute for the Study of War. They suggested Ukrainian forces still held the street where my grandparents lived during the week they had died, although the front line had been shifting rapidly.

My colleagues helped me identify the Russian military units that went on to capture Dachne. We found telephone numbers of Russian soldiers. But none of them agreed to speak to me.

I turned to the Ukrainian military.

A soldier from the 33rd Mechanised Brigade, who gave his name simply as Vlad, stated his unit had still been in Dachne at the time my grandparents were believed to have died and that the Russians had been swiftly advancing.

Another Ukrainian soldier I spoke to also confirmed Ukraine's troops had still been in control of some parts of Dachne in late January.

We put our findings on the deaths of my grandparents to the Ukrainian military.

It remarked it had no verified evidence on how they died, or which implicated its servicemen during the "intense hostilities". It added that investigating allegations of wrongdoing was the role of law enforcement.

We also approached Russia's Ministry of Defence and Russia's embassy in London for comment - they did not respond.

Sisters Sasha (right) and Anastasiya were reunited at Belgrade Airport.

The Donetsk regional prosecutor's office, which is now based outside Russian-controlled territory, has documented alleged Russian war crimes reported by eyewitnesses in villages around Dachne during December 2024 and January 2025 - including the killing of five civilians in a basement in the nearby village of Kostyantynopilske.

In a recent development, however, Ukrainian investigators have no equivalent cases registered in Dachne during that period. They have documented only three deaths there. My father and grandparents are not among them.

Their bodies lie in occupied territory, and I do not know if I will ever be able to say goodbye properly and bury them with dignity.

There is little more I can do for them, except one thing - mend my relationship with my sister and my mother.

Almost three years after I last saw my sister, I fly to Belgrade where she now lives.

Anastasiya (left) and her sister Sasha look through photos of their father.

According to recent reports, she is waiting for me at the airport, holding lilies, and a plate with a silly nickname on it that she gave me when we were children. We hug, cry and laugh. It feels as if something between us is finally falling back into place.

At her flat, we look through family photographs and talk about my investigation and what I was able to find. My grief is still there, but it hurts a little less. I'm no longer carrying it alone.

"Are you ready?" Sasha asks. She rings our mother - who has also moved to Serbia - and puts the phone on speaker.

Sources indicate that "Hi, Mum. It's Nastya," I say. First there is silence. Then I hear her crying. "Nastya, my darling, hello," she replies.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple's next iPhone release (probably) isn't until sometime next year, but that doesn't mean leaks aren't coming in hot and ready for our perusal.

The latest leak about Apple's flagship hardware product concerns the rumored iPhone 18e. According to digital renders of the device seen by Engadget, you can expect the next budget iPhone to have a camera bump that looks quite different from the iPhone 17e that introduced earlier this year.

While the 17e has only a single camera lens flush with the phone's back, Engadget's source suggests that Apple is looking to give the 18e a camera plateau similar to the one on the iPhone Pro models.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

By that, we mean it will allegedly house the camera lens in a nearly square-shaped module measuring about 28 by 35mm. Alongside the lens, the housing will contain the LED flash and a rear microphone. Yes, to be as abundantly clear as possible, Apple is apparently still sticking with just one camera lens here, even if the phone might look like it has more going on back there this time around.

Interestingly, Engadget's report goes further, as they also saw renders of the still-not-available base iPhone 18 and the next iPhone Air. The iPhone 18 reportedly looks similar to previous models, with a thicker camera module. However, the iPhone Air 2 renders show a second camera lens on that phone. As you may or may not recall, the previous iPhone Air model only had one lens, so that would be a pretty substantial upgrade for that device.

We don't know for certain when these devices will actually launch, but previous reporting suggests that we should see some or all of them by the end of March 2027. They may or may not launch alongside a new MacBook Neo and some new iPad models.

Trump boosts Nvidia boss return but are US politicians on board?

After the AI chipmaker Nvidia confirmed it was bringing back embattled former head Jensen Huang and the manufacturer's stock shot up like a bullet, President Donald Trump took a very public victory lap.

"I made the deal," he said during a lengthy phone interview with cable business news channel CNBC.

Sources indicate that trump followed that with an AI-generated image posted to his social media platform that riffed on the famous photograph taken moments after the 2024 attempt on his life in Pennsylvania. But instead of Trump in the image, Huang was the one surrounded by Secret Service guards. It depicted him in front of an Nvidia banner - with a raised first clenching a red bra.

The post was classic Trump â potentially offensive, yet still a bit opaque.

Was Trump suggesting Huang survived a scandal â one that includes allegations of recklessly jeopardising US national security by consorting with a suspected Chinese spy â the way he had survived an assassin's bullet?

Was the bra a celebration Huang's reported extramarital affairs? By replacing the US flag with an Nvidia standard, was he claiming that America and one of its largest, most powerful companies are one and the same?

At the very least, the image underscores how inextricably linked Huang and Trump now are, with the fate of the former hinging on the successes and failures of the latter.

And with that comes significant risks for the American president and for Republicans, including Vice-President JD Vance, who played a key part in his efforts to rescue Huang.

While Trump has said that a "very thorough investigation" by federal officials "exonerated" Huang and his reinstatement poses no national security threat, that is far from the final word on the matter.

"Every time you have a Chinese woman that's good looking or beautiful, they say she's a spy," Trump told CNBC, adding that "with Jensen, I don't believe that's true".

Democrats and some concerned Republicans in Congress have a different view.

They are promising to launch their own oversight of Huang and Nvidia, with subpoenas and compelled witness testimony, in order to assess whether they violated laws by allowing China to access sophisticated microchip technology.

State governments could also launch their own investigations.

Any newly introduced revelations could further damage the organization's standing â and, by association, Trump himself.

"I have warned the administration from the start about Communist China obtaining our most advanced chips through both smuggling and remote access," Republican Senator Tom Cotton posted on X.

"Congress has much to investigate," he noted.

Faisal Islam: Fears over the AI boom haven't gone away.

What Jensen Huang's return teaches China's Xi about Trump.

US attorney general dodges questions about Nvidia investigation.

While Huang has a long record of success at Nvidia, there is no guarantee that he can recapture past glory now that his star his dimmed.

Even if he is free from any criminal liability, the tech mogul is about to be in a much harsher spotlight than he has ever experienced.

Trump also appears to be on the wrong side of public opinion when it comes to AI writ large.

In the recent US midterm elections, candidates on both the left and right campaigned on imposing fresh restrictions on data centre construction, with many calling for new legal guardrails to prevent AI-fuelled economic and social disruption.

"Rather than addressing the American people's growing concerns about AI, this administration remains asleep at the wheel or willfully ignorant as our most advanced technologies fall into the hands of our greatest competitors," congresswoman Sydney Kamlager-Dove, a California Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, told the BBC.

The president's own political base is also suspicious of the latest technology, with rural conservatives often rebelling at the demands that massive tech companies have placed on their local resources and civic infrastructure.

How Nvidia is reacting to Jensen Huang's return as CEO.

The Nvidia story has also exposed rifts in Trump's own administration, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, a China hawk, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, a vocal proponent of AI, publicly feuding over whether to impose new restrictions on AI chip exports.

Both Bessent and Lutnick travelled with Trump on his recent trip to China, although it was the commerce secretary who hitched a ride back to the White House on the Marine One helicopter when Trump returned to Washington last Thursday.

Polling also indicated that political corruption was a top problem for voters this year.

The president's willingness to intervene in the deliberations of a major private manufacturer in which he owns millions of dollars of stock could further fuel those concerns.

Trump's decision to help save Huang â noting on Monday that "we have to protect our geniuses, and he certainly is a genius" â could further inflame the public's sense that the rich and powerful, genius or not, play by a different set of rules.

"It almost feels like they've bent the rule, the regulation, to allow this to happen because it's such an key part of our economy right now," Steve Bannon, a former top Trump adviser, stated on his podcast on Monday.

"Even in the crash of 2008... I never saw the government step in and take over a board of directors.".

For this American president, however, these risks appear to be worth taking because of the stakes involved.

Trump has long viewed the success of the US economy as a key part of his political legacy.

He boasted of the historic growth and low unemployment during his first presidential term (while glossing over the disruptions caused by the Covid pandemic).

And since returning to office, he has celebrated as major US stock indices posted new record highs.

Recent US economic expansion has been fuelled largely by investment in AI technology, and Trump has become one of the industry's biggest boosters.

He scolded states and local governments for blocking data centre construction and predicted that the nation that wins the race for supremacy in AI â which he has tried to rebrand as "super intelligence" â will control the fate of the world.

If Trump views the economy as the key to his political success and AI as instrumental to the health of the US economy, then his dramatic, precedent-shattering actions to try to rescue Nvidia, the company at the centre of America's AI industry, make more sense.

In the weeks since concerns over Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy first surfaced, Nvidia's stock price tumbled more than 32%.

Last Friday alone, it fell 14%.

US stock indices tumbled as well, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq down 10% last week and the larger S&P 500 dropping 8.6%.

The recent financial turmoil may have given Trump a glimpse into a future where AI growth is just the latest financial bubble â like the housing market in 2008 and internet companies in 2001 â that is due for a resounding pop, with similarly dire economic consequences to follow.

Trump's intervention on behalf of Huang arrested that drop, at least for a day.

On Tuesday, Nvidia's stock price gave back much of the bounce it had enjoyed, and larger stock indices were mixed. The fate of the America economy and the AI juggernaut that has powered it is still undetermined.

Trump's intervention may not be a crisis fully averted, but only a crisis delayed.

And if an AI reckoning does come, the US president will be hard-pressed to avoid being caught in the maelstrom.

Tech Report: iRestore Elite Laser Hair Growth System Review: Husband-Approved

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1347 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s jarring, for example, when the luscious, flowing locks of your youth start to disappear before your very eyes.
  • It has been revealed that I learned about iRestore’s Elite Laser Growth Hair System after it came across my TikTok FYP.
  • However, an even better test subject stood before me: my sweet husband, who is dealing with a rapidly receding hairline.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Aging Process is hard. It’s jarring, for example, when the luscious, flowing locks of your youth start to disappear before your very eyes. But there's nothing to do about this natural hair loss—or is there? While still the subject of ongoing research, red-light therapy has been used to treat inflammation, pain relief, and wrinkles, and—as it turns out—it may also help with hair regrowth. It’s also a much more accessible option than flying to Istanbul for a full-on hair transplant.

It has been revealed that I learned about iRestore’s Elite Laser Growth Hair System after it came across my TikTok FYP. My algorithm likely served it to me because of my own hair woes (scalp irritation and eczema). Upon learning more about the system, I hoped it could help me with cell regeneration and kill off the bacteria causing flares on my scalp.

However, an even better test subject stood before me: my sweet husband, who is dealing with a rapidly receding hairline. So I roped him into testing this laser helmet—for science, of course. And to better understand mentioned science, I spoke with Zakia Rahman, MD, FAAD, a clinical professor of dermatology at Stanford University School of Medicine.

In a recent development, red-light therapy didn’t start as a treatment for antiaging and recovery. It actually came about as an accidental solution for hair loss in the 1960s, when Hungarian scientist Endre Mester was researching whether exposure to red light could treat cancer in hairless mice. Imagine his surprise when the mice started growing hair.

It has been revealed that red-light therapy has come a long way since then. According to Rahman, red-light wavelengths are thought to activate the mitochondria in skin cells, which may encourage an uptick in the production of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) to promote new growth. Red-light therapy may also improve blood flow to hair follicles.

According to recent reports, importantly, iRestore's devices are FDA-cleared—a safety designation from the US Food and Drug Administration indicating that a product is “substantially equivalent” to another legally marketed device. There are three hair-growth devices in iRestore's lineup: the entry-level Essential ($425), the mid-tier Professional ($799), and the Elite ($1,699). Each contains iRestore’s proprietary Lumitech technology, which combines LED lights and medical-grade lasers. These laser diodes, called Vixo lasers, operate in the range of 655 to 680 nanometers (nm). (Preliminary studies with mice have shown that using red light in the 600- to 660-nm range, and infrared wavelengths in the 800- to 850-nm range, can promote cell regeneration, pain relief, and more.).

The idea is that this dynamic duo of lights and lasers can penetrate deeper into the skin than ordinary red light with lasers, while the LEDs ensure light is distributed across the scalp for maximum efficacy. Together, they reach a maximum of 2,500 milliwatts (mW) in the Elite, compared to the Professional's 1,410 mW and Essential's 600 mW.

The Elite is iRestore’s top-of-the-line offering and has the most LEDs of the three laser hair-growth systems, with 500 diodes in total—that's 300 lasers and 200 LEDs. The Essential has 51 lasers and 69 LEDs for a total of 120 diodes, while the iRestore Professional has 82 lasers and 200 LEDs for a total of 282 diodes. The Elite was also designed to cover more of the scalp than the other two models and requires 12 minutes of daily use, while the Professional and Essential require 25 minutes every other day.

If price is not a factor, the Elite is the no-brainer choice due to its higher-concentrated light therapy, shorter use time, and potentially faster results.

The helmet arrived in hefty red packaging containing the helmet, a portable battery pack (annoyingly, this is a $99 add-on purchase), a charging cord, and a red-and-black zippered travel case. It feels very fragile, and I wouldn't throw it around—then again, you probably wouldn't blueprint to shove such an expensive device in the back of your bathroom vanity.

According to recent reports, during the daily 12-minute sessions with the Elite helmet, you'll feel as if you're sitting under bright, hot sunlight. The remote displays a countdown of how many minutes you have left, and it beeps once the cycle is complete. Because I was testing the helmet to treat my dry scalp and eczema, I grew increasingly concerned with every passing minute of feeling warmer and warmer. (Sweating is a significant no-no for eczema, so I wasn’t thrilled to experience this side effect.) With time, my husband was able to get used to the heat-lamp effect, as it’s not painful, just initially uncomfortable.

Within the first two weeks of continuously using the helmet, I was thrilled to see baby hairs begin to pop up around my husband's hairline. The growth continued through two months of regular use. The top of his crown had more volume and overall hair density, while fresh growth appeared in the more drastically affected areas near his forehead. While the additional hair didn’t completely cover his scalp, the change was stark enough for old college friends and family members to remark on how good his hair looked.

According to recent reports, the effects aren't permanent, though. Unfortunately, my husband stopped his iRestore routine after a few months due to travel. While the iRestore Elite comes with a case that makes it super portable, my husband was nervous about misplacing it while we were on the go. (Also, the thing takes up a decent amount of space.) Unfortunately, stopping the treatments reversed the progress in a matter of weeks. Just like that, he was back to square one.

In a recent development, rahman likens this phenomenon to the importance of a commitment to a healthy daily diet and regular exercise; one instance of either won't make a difference in your health. Rather, consistency is required to drive results. When I told her that my husband's hair growth had fallen off, she strongly encouraged us to pick it back up.

In addition to using the red-light therapy helmet as recommended, iRestore suggests adding thickening haircare products (shampoo, conditioner, supplements, and serum) to your regimen to get the best results. The star ingredient in the serum and shampoo is plant-based Redensyl, which is meant to fortify hair follicles during their regrowth. Additional elements—like the shampoo's castor oil and biotin, and the conditioner's vegan keratin and argan oil—act as natural strengtheners.

Sources indicate that the supplements contain natural dihydrotestosterone (DHT) blockers derived from saw palmetto. These blockers work to prevent the enzyme (5-alpha reductase) from transforming testosterone into DHT. In essence, this hormone is a driver of pattern hair loss and can lead to general inactivity in hair growth.

The supplements, strengthening serum, shampoo, and conditioner come included with the purchase of the iRestore Elite. The extras didn't seem to boost my results but may have supported my husband's regular use of the helmet. (Full disclosure: He was also using his usual Rogaine throughout this entire process.).

Ultimately, these included products are a nice bonus, but you don't need to go out of your way to buy them from iRestore or to replenish your stash. Plenty of anti-hair-loss treatments are available, including oral and topical medications and hair-transplant procedures. All have their merits in slowing hair thinning and promoting fuller hair. Even so, “combination therapy will work better than a stand-alone," notes Rahman, in response to my question about whether red-light therapy could work as an isolated treatment or if it's best to include it as part of a multicomponent regimen. Essentially, the potential benefits of red-light therapy only stand to increase when you supplement it with minoxidil and other highly researched hair-loss measures.

As for my eczema, the iRestore Elite did quell my scalp flare-ups, but I don't think I'd throw down so much money for just that. For hair regrowth, that's a totally different story. My husband was already using Rogaine before the iRestore Elite revealed up. But combined with the helmet and iRestore's hair-growth products and supplements, he experienced greater results. For those pursuing thicker hair at home, the iRestore Elite is surprisingly effective.

Super Bowl 61 will be telecast live in hundreds of Imax theaters in February via a partnership with the NFL and Disney's ESPN, which has the broadcast rights to the 2027 game.

It marks the largest Imax live event in the manufacturer's history and the first time that the Super Bowl will be available in the format, according to a news release.

Sources indicate that the four-hour event on Feb. 14 will include ESPN's main Super Bowl game telecast, as well as Jay-Z's halftime performance and pregame and postgame coverage.

Sources indicate that tickets will be available for theaters in the United States and select international markets, including Australia, Fresh Zealand and Brazil. Tickets are expected to go on sale in January. Pricing was not disclosed.

"Watching the Super Bowl with your fellow fans is one of the great shared experiences in sports, and this first-of-its-kind collaboration with the NFL and IMAX takes it to a historic fresh scale," noted Ken Potrock, president of major event integration for The Walt Disney Co.

In addition to ESPN channels, this season's championship game will also be available on streaming platform Disney+ as well as Disney's broadcast network ABC.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The late Pope Francis suffered a spiritual crisis during his papacy when he struggled with how to lead the Catholic Church and believed he saw and heard the devil on several occasions, according to an annotated collection of his private diaries published on Tuesday.
  • Francis was pope for 12 years until his death last April.
